cards.title: Observability — What It Actually Means
cards.teaser: Observability is not a tool category or a vendor pitch. It is a property of a system: the degree to which you can understand its internal state purely by examining its external outputs. If you have to deploy a special build to answer a question, your system is not observable.

runs.text: The term comes from control theory. Rudolf Kálmán defined observability in 1960 as a property of a dynamic system: a system is observable if, given a finite sequence of outputs, you can reconstruct the full internal state. Charity Majors and the Honeycomb team carried that definition into software engineering intact.

The engineering definition: an observable system is one where you can ask arbitrary questions about its runtime behavior — questions you did not think to ask when you wrote the code — and answer them from the data already being emitted. You do not need a new deploy. You do not need to add logging statements. You do not need to reproduce the issue locally.

That last clause is what separates observability from monitoring. Monitoring tells you when things you already anticipated go wrong. Observability lets you investigate things you did not anticipate. Monitoring is a
known-unknown
tool. Observability handles
unknown-unknowns

Honeycomb's framing, from Observability Engineering (Majors, Fong-Jones, Miranda, 2022): "Observability is a measure of how well you can understand and explain any state your system can get into, no matter how novel or bizarre." Novel is the operative word. If you can only explain states you anticipated, you are monitoring, not observing.
A system is observable if you can figure out what is happening inside it just by looking at what comes out — without having to add more instrumentation or redeploy to investigate.

cards.title: Monitoring vs Observability — Known-Unknowns vs Unknown-Unknowns
cards.teaser: Monitoring answers questions you thought to ask. Observability answers questions you did not know you needed to ask. The difference is not a tooling upgrade — it is a fundamental shift in what your data model allows you to do.

runs.text: Monitoring is built around known failure modes. You decide, in advance, which metrics matter: CPU utilization, error rate, p99 latency. You set thresholds. You fire alerts when thresholds are crossed. Monitoring works well for the failures you have seen before and thought to model.

Observability is built for failure modes you have not seen. In complex distributed systems, the most damaging incidents are never the ones that triggered your existing alerts cleanly. They are the interactions you did not model — the user whose specific combination of account flags, region, and feature-flag state causes a code path that no alert watches.

items.text: "Is error rate above 1%?" — a question formulated before the incident.
"Which user_id, region, and feature_flag combination is responsible for the elevated error rate?" — a question formulated during the incident.

runs.text: The comparison table:

items.text: Monitoring — pre-aggregated, low-cardinality, threshold-based, alert-driven, designed for known failure modes
Observability — high-cardinality raw events, exploratory queries, designed for unknown failure modes
Monitoring data model: a number over time (a metric). Observability data model: a structured event with many dimensions.
Monitoring answer: yes/no (threshold crossed). Observability answer: the exact subset of requests or users exhibiting the problem.

runs.text: Observability does not replace monitoring. Dashboards and alerts on known signals are still valuable. The mistake is believing that more monitoring — more dashboards, more alerts — eventually becomes observability. It does not. Observability requires a different data model, not more of the same data.
Monitoring is a checklist of things you already know to watch. Observability lets you ask questions you didn't write down in advance. You need both — but they are not the same tool.

cards.title: The Three Pillars — and Why the Framing Is Incomplete
cards.teaser: Logs, metrics, and traces are called the three pillars of observability. The framing is useful for introduction — and subtly wrong as a destination. The pillars are signal types that overlap in awkward ways; treating them as separate silos creates the gaps incidents fall into.

runs.text: The three pillars taxonomy comes from Peter Bourgon's 2017 blog post and was popularized by the CNCF observability landscape. Each pillar captures a distinct signal type:

items.text: — timestamped, structured or unstructured records of discrete events. What happened and when. Rich in context when structured; expensive to query at volume.
— numeric measurements aggregated over time. Cheap to store, fast to query, alertable. Low in cardinality by design — you pre-aggregate away the dimensions you did not anticipate needing.

— records of the causal chain of a single request as it moves through distributed services. A trace is a tree of spans, each span representing a unit of work with a start time, end time, and attributes.

runs.text: The critique: these three pillars overlap significantly, and the silos create operational problems. A structured log event looks a lot like a trace span. A metric derived from log parsing is slow and fragile. A trace without associated logs lacks the context to explain why a span was slow. When each pillar lives in a different tool, with a different data model, cross-pillar correlation requires manual effort — and manual effort during an incident is exactly what you cannot afford.
Honeycomb's argument, which OpenTelemetry has partially validated, is that the unified abstraction is the
event

: a wide, structured record with a timestamp, a duration, and many fields. Logs, traces, and metrics are all derivable from events. The pillar model is a historical artifact of which data stores were built first, not a fundamental taxonomy.

OpenTelemetry (OTEL) is the CNCF project working toward a unified instrumentation API and data model. It defines trace, metric, and log signals under one SDK — a practical acknowledgment that the three-pillar silos are an implementation problem, not a conceptual one.

Logs, metrics, and traces describe different shapes of the same underlying reality. The three-pillar model is a useful introduction but a poor architecture goal — the gaps between three separate silos are where incidents hide.

cards.title: The Four Golden Signals
cards.teaser: Google's Site Reliability Engineering book defined four signals that, taken together, cover nearly all production health: latency, traffic, errors, and saturation. If you can only instrument four things, instrument these. If you instrument more, these four are the baseline everything else extends.

runs.text: The four golden signals come from Chapter 6 of Google's SRE book (Beyer et al., 2016). They emerged from Google's own experience running global-scale production systems and were chosen because they are collectively sufficient to detect most user-facing degradation.

items.text: — how long it takes to serve a request. Distinguish success latency from error latency: a request that fails fast looks fine on p99 but is masking a problem. Track p50, p95, p99 — averages hide tail behavior.
— how much demand is being placed on the system. Requests per second, queries per second, messages per second. Traffic is the denominator for error rate and the predictor of saturation.

— the rate of requests that fail, explicitly (HTTP 5xx) or implicitly (HTTP 200 with a wrong response body). Implicit errors are the dangerous ones: they pass your error-rate alert and fail your users silently.

— how full the system's most constrained resource is. CPU and memory are the usual suspects, but the actual bottleneck is often a thread pool, a connection pool, or a queue depth. Saturation is a leading indicator: it degrades before latency and errors do.

runs.text: The golden signals are intentionally high-level. They do not tell you why something is wrong — they tell you that something is wrong and give you the starting coordinate for investigation. You then reach for traces, logs, and high-cardinality event data to answer the why.

Google's SRE book advises: if you are only going to monitor four things per service, monitor the golden signals. Most production outages are visible in at least one of them before users start filing tickets.
Latency, traffic, errors, saturation: these four numbers tell you if a service is healthy. They don't tell you why it isn't, but they tell you where to start looking.

cards.title: RED Method — Rate, Errors, Duration
cards.teaser: The RED method is the four golden signals simplified for services: Rate (how many requests per second?), Errors (how many are failing?), Duration (how long do they take?). Tom Wilkie's formulation is the practical starting point for instrumenting any microservice.

runs.text: Tom Wilkie of Grafana Labs introduced the RED method as a service-focused simplification. Where the four golden signals cover both services and the underlying resources they depend on, RED focuses exclusively on the service layer.

items.text: — requests per second the service is handling. Answers: "is there traffic?" and "how much?"
— number (or percentage) of requests that fail. Encompasses explicit HTTP errors, business-logic errors, and timeout failures.

— distribution of time each request takes. Equivalent to latency; the word "duration" is preferred because it is more precise — it is the time a request spent being processed by this service, not the round-trip time as seen by the client.

runs.text: RED is particularly well-suited to microservice architectures because it applies uniformly across all services in the call graph. You can apply the same dashboard template to every service without customization. Anomalies surface as deviations from baseline Rate, spikes in Errors, or shifts in Duration distributions.
RED is incomplete for resource-level investigation. It tells you when a database call is slow but not whether the database itself is near saturation. That is where the USE method applies.

Prometheus and Grafana are built around RED by convention. The standard Prometheus histogram metric — request_duration_seconds — gives you Duration; a counter on total requests gives you Rate; a counter on error responses gives you Errors. The three together are the minimum viable dashboard for any service.
RED is the three questions every service should be able to answer: how busy am I, how often do I fail, and how long does each request take? Those three numbers tell you whether a service is healthy.

cards.title: USE Method — Utilization, Saturation, Errors
cards.teaser: The USE method is Brendan Gregg's framework for analyzing resource bottlenecks: Utilization (how busy is the resource?), Saturation (how much work is queued?), Errors (how many errors has it produced?). RED answers "is my service healthy?"; USE answers "why is my hardware struggling?"

runs.text: Brendan Gregg, performance engineer at Netflix (and later Sun/Oracle), developed the USE method to provide a systematic way to characterize any resource in a system. Where RED focuses on services (requests in, responses out), USE focuses on infrastructure: CPUs, memory, disks, network interfaces, connection pools.

items.text: — average time the resource was busy serving work, as a percentage. A CPU at 90% utilization is heavily loaded. Critically: utilization alone does not indicate a problem — a CPU can be at 90% utilization with zero queued work. It becomes a problem when paired with saturation.

— the degree to which the resource has more work than it can handle: queue depth, wait time, or the number of processes blocked on the resource. Saturation is the leading indicator of degradation. A saturated connection pool will cause timeouts before error rates in the application layer rise.

— error events from the resource itself: ECC memory errors, disk read errors, network packet drops, TCP retransmissions. These are often invisible to application-layer monitoring but precede hardware failures.

runs.text: The USE method works well in practice because it is a complete checklist. For every resource in the system — apply USE. If utilization is low, saturation is zero, and errors are absent, that resource is not the bottleneck. Move on. If saturation is high, you have found a constraint worth investigating.

Gregg's original USE method article (brendangregg.com/usemethod.html) includes a resource list for Linux: CPUs, memory capacity, network interfaces, storage devices, storage controllers, and more. Each maps directly to USE metrics available from the OS. It is the basis for node-exporter in the Prometheus ecosystem.

USE is a checklist for diagnosing hardware and resource problems. For every resource, ask: how busy is it, is work piling up waiting for it, and is it producing errors? If all three are low, that resource isn't your problem.

cards.title: Cardinality — The Core Concept
cards.teaser: Cardinality is the number of unique values a label or field can take. It is the single most important concept for understanding the cost structure of observability tooling — and the reason why adding a user_id label to a metric can destroy a Prometheus instance.

runs.text: In mathematics, the cardinality of a set is its number of elements. In the context of observability:

items.text: (200, 404, 500 — a few dozen possible values) or

runs.text: Why cardinality matters to cost: time-series databases like Prometheus store one series per unique label combination. If you have a metric with labels
service
(10 values) ×
endpoint
(100 values) ×
status_code
(20 values), you have 20,000 time series. Add a
user_id
label with 1,000,000 unique users and you now have 20 billion potential time series. Prometheus will OOM before you finish the thought.

This is the fundamental tension in observability: the dimensions that are most useful for debugging (user_id, request_id, session_id) are exactly the dimensions that traditional time-series metrics cannot handle. This tension is what drove Honeycomb to build around high-cardinality event storage instead of a Prometheus-style metrics store.

Prometheus explicitly documents high cardinality as a performance antipattern. The Prometheus best practices guide states: "Labels should not include unbounded values like user IDs, email addresses, or other strings with high cardinality." The rule exists because violating it causes out-of-memory crashes in production.

Cardinality is how many different values a label can have. Low cardinality (status codes: a dozen values) is cheap. High cardinality (user IDs: millions of values) is expensive. Traditional metrics databases break at high cardinality — which is exactly why they can't help you debug per-user problems.

cards.title: High-Cardinality Fields and the Wide-Events Approach
cards.teaser: user_id, request_id, and span_id are high-cardinality fields — they have millions of unique values and are completely off-limits in traditional metrics. The wide-events approach, championed by Honeycomb, solves this by storing structured events with all fields together rather than pre-aggregating them away.

runs.text: High-cardinality fields are the most valuable fields for debugging. When production breaks, the first question is almost always "which users are affected?" — and that requires
user_id
. The second question is "what were those specific requests?" — and that requires
request_id
. The third is "which spans in the trace were slow?" — requiring
span_id
. All three are high-cardinality. Traditional metrics cannot store them.

Wide events are Honeycomb's answer to this constraint. Instead of emitting many narrow metrics (one per signal, with pre-aggregated label values), emit one wide, structured event per request containing every relevant field: user_id, endpoint, duration, status_code, feature_flags, tenant_id, plan_type, geographic region, browser version, and anything else you might ever want to filter by.

The key insight: when all fields travel together in a single event, you can slice the dataset by any combination of dimensions at query time. You never have to decide in advance which dimensions matter. The query engine handles the aggregation — not the instrumentation code.

items.text: http_requests_total{status="500", endpoint="/checkout"} = 42. You cannot break this down by user_id after the fact — it was aggregated away.
One structured JSON event per request with 50+ fields. At query time, filter to status=500 AND endpoint=/checkout AND user_id=specific_user. No pre-aggregation needed.

runs.text: Honeycomb was founded on the premise that the most useful debugging data — high-cardinality, high-dimensionality events — was being thrown away by every existing monitoring tool. Their columnar storage engine (backed by a custom query engine called Retriever) was purpose-built to make wide-event queries fast at production volumes.

A wide event is one fat record per request containing every field you might ever want — user ID, endpoint, duration, flags, everything. Because nothing is pre-aggregated, you can slice and filter by any combination of fields when you're debugging, not just the dimensions you predicted in advance.

cards.title: The Cost of Cardinality
cards.teaser: Every unique label combination in a time-series database becomes a separate series. The index storing those series is what causes out-of-memory events, slow queries, and five-figure infrastructure bills. Understanding the cardinality math is the difference between a healthy Prometheus and one that falls over at 3 AM.

runs.text: Cardinality has three concrete costs in production observability systems:

items.text: Prometheus keeps an in-memory inverted index of all active time series. Each unique label set — the combination of all label key-value pairs for one series — occupies memory in this index. At 10,000 active series the index is fast and small. At 10,000,000 active series it consumes gigabytes of RAM and makes every query scan expensive.

PromQL and similar query languages operate over the full time-series index. A query for sum(http_requests_total) over a million series is far slower than the same query over ten thousand. High-cardinality label combinations degrade dashboard render times and alert evaluation latency — which means alerts fire late when you are already under load.

Managed time-series databases (Datadog, Grafana Cloud, New Relic) charge per active series or per data point ingested. A label with 1,000,000 unique values multiplied across every metric that carries it produces billions of series-minutes per month. The bills are real. Teams have been surprised by 10x cost spikes from a single label change.

runs.text: The Prometheus documentation describes "cardinality explosion" as the primary cause of Prometheus performance degradation in production. The phrase is apt: cardinality grows multiplicatively. Two labels each with 1,000 values produces 1,000,000 combinations. Three such labels produces 1,000,000,000.

Datadog's pricing model explicitly counts custom metrics. In 2022, several engineering teams reported monthly bills increasing by $50,000–$100,000 after a developer added a customer_id label to a high-throughput metric without understanding the cardinality implications. The metric had to be deleted and re-instrumented without the label.

Each unique label combination is a separate time series, and time series cost memory, query time, and money. Cardinality grows by multiplication — two labels with 1,000 values each means a million series. That math is why a single bad label can make Prometheus fall over.

cards.title: Cardinality Explosion — Common Causes
cards.teaser: Cardinality explosions are not theoretical. They happen regularly in production and they follow predictable patterns: someone adds a user-scoped label, a URL path leaks query parameters, a trace ID ends up in a metric, or a dynamic value slips into a label. Knowing the patterns is how you prevent them.

runs.text: A cardinality explosion is when the number of active time series in a metrics store grows unexpectedly and rapidly, consuming resources faster than the system can handle. The common triggers:

items.text: directly to a metric. These labels grow with your user base — a SaaS product with 500,000 customers produces 500,000 series per metric that carries the label.
Using raw request paths as label values:
is a unique path for every user-order pair. The correct approach: parameterize to
Trace or request IDs in metrics.
is unique per request — infinite cardinality. Metrics instruments occasionally get these added by developers who are thinking about tracing, not metrics.

Using the raw error string (which may contain IDs, timestamps, or variable data) as a label value. Error strings should be classified into a small set of error types before being used as metric labels.
Any label value that contains a timestamp or version string will create new series continuously, with old series never expiring until the TSDB's retention period elapses.

runs.text: Prevention is mechanical: any label whose value set is bounded and small (fewer than a few hundred unique values) is safe. Any label whose value set is user-determined, request-determined, or otherwise unbounded is dangerous. Most metric client libraries provide no guardrails — the discipline must come from code review and instrumentation standards.

Cardinality explosions happen when a label can take on an unlimited number of values — a user ID, a raw URL path, a request ID. Each new value creates a new time series. The fix is almost always to parameterize or classify the label value into a small, bounded set.

cards.title: Sampling — Head vs Tail
cards.teaser: At high traffic volumes, collecting every trace is prohibitively expensive. Sampling keeps a representative subset. Head sampling decides at the start of a request; tail sampling decides at the end, after you know whether it was interesting. The choice between them determines whether you can find your rare, slow, or failed requests.

runs.text: A service handling 10,000 requests per second cannot afford to store traces for all of them. Sampling is the mechanism for keeping costs bounded while preserving signal. Two fundamental strategies:

items.text: — the sampling decision is made at the beginning of the request, before any processing occurs. Typically a probability: sample 1% of all requests uniformly. Simple, cheap, and consistent — all spans in a sampled trace are kept. The fatal flaw: rare events (errors, slow outliers) are also sampled at 1%, meaning you miss 99% of the incidents you most need to investigate.

— the sampling decision is made after the request completes, once you know its outcome. Keep 100% of traces where status=error or duration > p99. Sample 1% of everything else. You preserve the interesting events and discard the boring fast-success requests. Cost: significantly more complex — a tail sampler must buffer all spans until the trace is complete before deciding.

runs.text: Most production observability pipelines combine both. Honeycomb's approach: use dynamic sampling with a per-key sample rate so that common, boring requests are heavily sampled while rare, interesting ones (errors, slow tails, specific user IDs) are sampled at 100%. OpenTelemetry Collector supports tail sampling via the tail-sampling processor.

Sampling is covered in depth in chapter 11 of this book. The key takeaway for this chapter: head sampling is cheap but makes incidents invisible; tail sampling is expensive but preserves the events that matter. At scale, naive head sampling is a false economy — you save storage costs but lose the ability to investigate the failures that cost you the most.

Head sampling flips a coin at the start of every request and stores the winners. Tail sampling waits until the request is done, then keeps it if it was slow or broken. Tail sampling is harder to build but keeps exactly the events you most need to debug.

cards.title: Wide Events — One Event with Many Fields
cards.teaser: The wide event is the atomic unit of observability in Honeycomb's model. One structured record per unit of work, containing every field you might ever want — not just the fields you thought you would need. The philosophy inverts the traditional instrumentation workflow: instrument everything once, query any slice later.

runs.text: In traditional monitoring, instrumentation is driven by known questions. You add a counter because you need to alert on error rate. You add a gauge because you want to track queue depth. Every metric answers a specific pre-formulated question.

Wide events invert this. The instrumentation question becomes: "what fields could matter in any future investigation?" Then you add all of them to a single structured event, emitted once per request (or once per unit of work for background jobs, queue workers, etc.).
A wide event for a checkout request might contain:

With 50 fields in a single event, any future investigation can filter and group by any combination of dimensions. The question "is the slowness affecting only users on the free plan, in eu-west-1, with the new checkout flow enabled?" is answerable without a new deploy, a new metric, or a new log line. The data is already there.

OpenTelemetry's semantic conventions are a standardized vocabulary for wide-event fields: http.request.method, user.id, server.address, and so on. Using the conventions means your events are queryable with the same field names across all services in the system.

A wide event is one JSON blob per request with every field that might ever be useful — user, region, feature flags, timing, status. Because all the data travels together, you can answer any combination of "who, where, when, what" questions without ever having to add more instrumentation.

cards.title: The Observability Spectrum — Black Box to Instrumented
cards.teaser: Observability is not binary. Systems exist on a spectrum from black box (you can only observe inputs and outputs) through white box (you can examine internal state) to fully instrumented (every significant operation emits structured, correlated telemetry). Most production systems sit somewhere in the middle — and knowing where you are is the first step to moving forward.

runs.text: The observability spectrum describes how much internal state a system exposes through its telemetry. It is useful for assessing a system's current state and prioritizing instrumentation work.

items.text: — you can only see external inputs and outputs. No logs, no metrics, no traces from inside the system. You know the system is down when users complain. Debugging means inference from external symptoms. This is the state of most third-party dependencies: you can observe the responses they return, but not their internal state.

— you can examine internal state, but passively. Logs exist but are unstructured; metrics exist but are not correlated to requests; no distributed tracing. You know what happened in individual components but cannot answer cross-service causality questions. The majority of systems that teams believe are "instrumented" are actually white box.

— structured logs, RED metrics per service, distributed traces across the call graph. You can answer: "which service is responsible for this latency increase?" Still missing: high-cardinality context that lets you answer "which specific requests or users are affected?"

— wide events with high-cardinality context, distributed traces that correlate to events, service-level objectives (SLOs) defined and measured. You can answer arbitrary questions about any production state, including states you never anticipated. This is the observability ideal described in Majors and Fong-Jones.

runs.text: Most engineering teams move along this spectrum incrementally. The practical journey: add structured logging first (cheap, high leverage). Add RED metrics per service. Add distributed tracing on the critical path. Add high-cardinality context to traces and events. Define SLOs. Most teams make it to structured telemetry and stop — full instrumentation requires a cultural commitment to treat observability as a first-class engineering concern, not an operational afterthought.

Majors and Fong-Jones argue that moving from white box to fully instrumented is not just a tooling change — it requires changing how engineers think about production. Instead of "my job ends when I merge" the posture becomes "my job includes understanding how this code behaves in production." That shift in responsibility is the real definition of the observability discipline.

The observability spectrum goes from black box (you can only see inputs and outputs) to fully instrumented (you can answer any question about what happened inside). Most systems are somewhere in the middle. The goal is to move right — not necessarily to perfection, but far enough to answer the questions that come up in incidents.
